The common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus) exhibits a suite of life-history traits that reflect its specialized sanguivorous diet and obligate sociality. Newborn pups emerge from the womb in an altricial state, weighing just 4 grams [Wwb = 4 grams], a modest mass that represents the energetic constraints of a pregnant female who must maintain flight capability throughout gestation. At a body temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], the gestation period lasts 189 days [tg = 189 days], a surprisingly long duration for a mammal of this adult size. This extended intrauterine development is likely linked to the challenges of supporting a foetus solely on a protein-rich but energetically dilute liquid diet. The investment of maternal resources during embryogenesis is intensive, as females must consume approximately half their own body mass in blood nightly to meet the combined metabolic demands of self-maintenance and foetal growth.

Adult body size in Desmodus rotundus is relatively modest, with the ultimate wet weight of mature individuals reaching approximately 33.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 33.2 grams]. This stable asymptotic body mass is achieved after a prolonged growth phase that spans many months. The forearm serves as a reliable index of structural size; the ultimate forearm-length in fully grown adults measures 5.8 cm [Li = 5.8 cm], a dimension that correlates strongly with flight efficiency and maneuverability during nocturnal foraging. Wing morphology is critical for the species' hovering and crawling locomotion on host animals. Comparative data indicate that these forearm dimensions are typical for phyllostomid bats of comparable body mass, though Desmodus rotundus exhibits slightly more robust wing elements to support its terrestrial locomotion habits when approaching sleeping prey on the ground.

Under the thermoneutral conditions of the roost, maintained at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], weaning occurs at 274 days since birth [tx = 274 days since birth], a remarkably extended period of maternal dependency. During this time, the pup progresses from exclusive milk ingestion to the ingestion of regurgitated blood provided by the mother, a process that involves cultural transmission of foraging site knowledge and prey recognition. The age at weaning documented in field studies contrasts sharply with anecdotal reports of 18 to 25 days found in some online sources, which likely represent the onset of solid food sampling rather than full nutritional independence. Total reliance on maternal provisioning for over nine months is among the longest lactation periods recorded for any bat species its size, highlighting the complexity of the social learning required for successful hematophagy.

Sexual maturation follows a comparably slow schedule. Puberty is attained at 285 days since birth [tp = 285 days since birth], when young bats reach the physiological capacity to reproduce under optimal roost conditions at 34 °C [T = 34 °C]. This timing means that most individuals do not commence reproductive activity until well into their second calendar year. The onset of puberty is tightly linked to the achievement of asymptotic body mass and the acquisition of foraging competence, as females must be able to feed themselves and a future dependent simultaneously. Delayed maturation is common among socially complex mammals, and Desmodus rotundus is no exception. The long juvenile period allows young individuals to refine the sophisticated social bonds and food-sharing networks that underpin cooperative foraging and allomaternal care observed in established colonies.

Under stable thermal conditions at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], each reproductive event yields a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and females typically produce around 2 litters per year [F_R_i = around 2 litters per year], though this frequency is contingent upon adequate food availability and stable roost temperatures. Life span in this species reaches 29.2 years [am = 29.2 years] under optimal captive or field conditions at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], an extremely long duration for a mammal of 33.2 grams adult body mass. This extended longevity places Desmodus rotundus among the longest-lived chiropterans relative to body size, a pattern consistent with the slow life-history syndrome observed in many tropical bat species where high adult survival, low fecundity, and prolonged maternal investment co-evolve under stable environmental conditions.
